<p class="lx-eyebrow">Six methods, what each asks and what it can tell a modeller</p><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table x6-fbt"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Method</th><th scope="col">Asks</th><th scope="col">Gives a model</th><th scope="col">Cannot tell</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Survey</td><td>How many, how much, how often, across a population.</td><td>Shares and rates by household group, such as who has a heat pump or who struggles with bills.</td><td>Why people act as they do, in depth; or whether a programme caused a change, without a comparison design.</td></tr><tr><td>Interview</td><td>Why and how, in people's own words.</td><td>Reasons, barriers and assumptions worth testing, including ones a model leaves out.</td><td>How common each view is across a city.</td></tr><tr><td>Choice experiment</td><td>Which trade-offs people accept.</td><td>How much each feature weighs, such as bill saving against control, for adoption scenarios.</td><td>What people do once the offer is real: the choices are stated, not observed.</td></tr><tr><td>Ethnography</td><td>How people live with energy, day to day.</td><td>Routines a model's behaviour rules should reflect, such as how heating is really used.</td><td>Numbers that hold for a whole city.</td></tr><tr><td>Policy analysis</td><td>How rules came about, and who shaped them.</td><td>The rules and limits a model must respect, and which of them are open to change.</td><td>How people experience the rules.</td></tr><tr><td>Participatory mapping</td><td>Which places matter to people, and why.</td><td>Layers to exclude or weigh in a siting screen, as in lesson A19.</td><td>How the whole population feels, when few take part.</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="lx-eyebrow">Six questions and the method that fits each best</p><ul><li>What share of Prairie City's households had trouble paying an energy bill last year, by income group? Survey.</li><li>Why do landlords turn down a free efficiency upgrade for their rental homes? Interview.</li><li>How much bill saving would a household trade for letting the utility adjust its thermostat at the peak? Choice experiment.</li><li>How do families actually use their heating through a winter, and what does comfort mean to them? Ethnography.</li><li>How did the state's rules for rooftop solar bill credits change over ten years, and who argued for what? Policy analysis.</li><li>Which places do residents want kept clear of a new solar farm, and why? Participatory mapping.</li></ul><p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you match the questions to methods, open each method, mark which involve people and test one survey result.</p>
<!-- x06-fallback:end -->
</div>
</div>

::: {#explain .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="x06-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- x06-ideas:start (written from the data by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<dl class="lx-ideas"><dt>Different questions</dt><dd>Each method answers its own kind of question: how many, why, which trade-off, how people live, how rules came about, which places matter.</dd><dt>For a modeller</dt><dd>Findings become inputs, household groups, behaviour rules, constraints, map layers or scenarios.</dd><dt>People first</dt><dd>Research with people needs informed consent and an ethics board's review before it starts.</dd><dt>Not causal by itself</dt><dd>A difference between joiners and others is not an effect; a fair comparison is a design choice of its own.</dd><dt>Neutral</dt><dd>No method is ranked above another here: each is the right tool for some questions and the wrong one for others.</dd></dl>
<!-- x06-ideas:end -->
</div>
</div>
<!-- x06-stop:start (written from the data by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-card xs-stop" id="x06-stop"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Where we stop</p><h3>This side topic stops at choosing a method</h3><p class="xs-stop-lede">Social-science methods enter the course as what each can tell a modeller and how to work with the people who use them; training in a method is beyond it.</p><div class="xs-stop-cols"><div><h4 class="xs-h">This side topic covers</h4><ul><li>What six methods answer, the data each needs and what each cannot tell.</li><li>Why research with people needs informed consent and an ethics board's review first.</li><li>How findings become a model's inputs, groups, layers or scenarios.</li></ul></div><div><h4 class="xs-h">Left to specialists</h4><ul><li>Training in any method: sampling, interview guides, experimental design, coding.</li><li>Designing questionnaires, choice sets or mapping workshops.</li><li>Fieldwork itself.</li></ul></div></div><h4 class="xs-h">Read next, three rungs</h4><ol class="xs-ladder"><li><b>Start here.</b> How energy social scientists choose and combine methods, with codes of practice for each family (open access). <span class="xs-src"><a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.erss.2018.07.007">Sovacool, Axsen and Sorrell (2018), Promoting novelty, rigor, and style in energy social science</a>, published 3 October 2018</span></li><li><b>Go further.</b> An introductory social-science research-methods textbook, for how each method is designed and judged. <span class="xs-src">Bryman, Social Research Methods (Oxford University Press), cited by name, any recent edition</span></li><li><b>Go deep.</b> The rules for research with people on DOE-supported projects: prior review and informed consent; your university's ethics board publishes its own guide. <span class="xs-src"><a href="https://www.energy.gov/documents/doe-o-443-1-dprotection-human-research-subjects2026-07-23pdf">U.S. Department of Energy, Order 443.1D, Protection of Human Research Subjects</a>, approved 5 August 2026</span></li></ol></div>
<!-- x06-stop:end -->
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Researcher</span>Working with social scientists</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li><b>Start together.</b> Bring a social scientist in while the question is being framed, not after the model is built.</li>
<li><b>Agree what the model needs.</b> Shares by group, weights, routines, rules or map layers, each with its units, date and population.</li>
<li><b>Review and consent first.</b> The ethics board reviews the plan before any data are collected; lesson R9 shows how.</li>
<li><b>Close the loop.</b> Tell participants what was found and how their answers were used.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

```{=html}
<p class="lx-lede">Two quick checks.</p>
<!-- x06-check:start (written from the data by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="x06-myth"><div class="lx-qq" data-id="volunteers" data-answer="myth"><p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “An online poll of 50 volunteers shows what share of a city's households struggle with their energy bills.”</p><ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Volunteers choose themselves; a share for the whole city needs a sample drawn to represent it, as large surveys such as EIA's do.</p></details></div></div><div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="x06"><div class="lx-qq" data-id="count" data-answer="a"><p class="lx-qtext">A modeller needs to know how many of a city's homes have a heat pump today, by income group. Which method fits best?</p><ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">A survey of a representative sample</li><li data-value="b">Ethnography in a few homes</li><li data-value="c">Interviews with installers</li></ul><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>A survey: a count by group across a population is what surveys do; ethnography and interviews explain how and why, in depth.</p></details></div></div>
<!-- x06-check:end -->
```
